# When the standard assumptions break {.divider background-color="#008CB7"}

[Act I · The tension]{.act}

## OLS gives the right line — but can lie about how sure we are

The classical standard-error formula assumes errors are independent and equally
spread. Real data rarely cooperate: cross-sections are **heteroskedastic**, grouped
data are **clustered**, time series are **autocorrelated**.

. . .

Under all three, OLS coefficients stay **unbiased** — the line is still right. What
breaks is the **standard error**: the $t$-stats, $p$-values, and intervals built on it
become untrustworthy. This chapter fixes the uncertainty, then asks what regression
can and cannot predict.

::: {.notes}
The headline mental model for the whole chapter: coefficients unchanged, inference repaired.
Everything in Act II is a different repair; Act III is about the limits that no repair removes.
:::

## Where we're going

::: {.incremental}
- **Repair the SEs** — heteroskedastic-robust (HC1), cluster-robust, and HAC (Newey–West)
- **Predict honestly** — the average outcome vs. one individual outcome
- **Know the floor** — why individual forecasts stay wide no matter the sample size
- **Watch the sample** — selection on $Y$ biases; selection on $X$ only costs precision
- **Judge estimators & tests** — BLUE, the bootstrap, and the power of a test
:::

## Six ideas anchor this chapter

::: {.incremental}
- **Robust SEs** — HC1 for heteroskedasticity; coefficients unchanged, only SEs move
- **Cluster-robust SEs** — errors correlated *within* groups, independent across them
- **Autocorrelation** — one period's error echoes into the next; fix with **HAC** SEs
- **CI for $E[Y\mid X^*]$** — the *average* outcome; shrinks to zero as $n\to\infty$
- **Prediction interval** — one *individual* outcome; the "$1+$" floor never disappears
- **Power $=1-\beta$** — the chance a true effect is actually detected
:::

[Coefficients stay put; this chapter is about trusting the numbers *around* them.]{.takeaway .fragment}

# Repairing the standard errors {.divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[Act II · The investigation]{.act}

## Three violations, three fixes — coefficients never change

::: {.incremental}
- **Heteroskedasticity** (error variance varies) — common in cross-sections → **HC1** robust SEs
- **Clustered errors** (correlated within groups) — panels, hierarchies → **cluster-robust** SEs
- **Autocorrelation** (errors correlated over time) — time series → **HAC (Newey–West)** SEs
:::

[The OLS point estimate is unbiased under all three. Only the standard error needs the correction.]{.takeaway .fragment}

## Robust SEs are one keyword: `vcov="HC1"`

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1|3-4|6-7|9-10|12"}
!pip install -q pyfixest                     # pyfixest isn't preinstalled in Colab (-q = quiet)

import pandas as pd                          # tabular data
import pyfixest as pf                         # pyfixest → OLS with robust SEs, R-style formulas

url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/data-open/master/AED/AED_HOUSE.DTA"
data = pd.read_stata(url)                    # 29 Davis, CA house sales (1999)

f = "price ~ size + bedrooms + bathrooms + lotsize + age + monthsold"
default = pf.feols(f, data=data)             # classical SEs (assume homoskedasticity)

robust = pf.feols(f, data=data, vcov="HC1")  # SAME coefficients, heteroskedastic-robust SEs
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
`vcov="HC1"` is the entire change. Point estimates are byte-for-byte identical to the default fit;
only `.se()`, `.tstat()`, `.pvalue()`, and `.confint()` differ.
:::

## For these houses, robust SEs tell the same story

Each extra square foot is worth about **\$68** in sale price, and it is strongly
significant either way: robust SE for `size` is **15.36** vs. default **15.39** ($p = 0.0002$).

. . .

The biggest adjustments are `bathrooms` (robust SE ~23% larger) and `lotsize` (~26%
smaller) — but both stay far from significance under either method.

[A rule of thumb: if robust SEs move more than ~30%, heteroskedasticity is real — report the robust ones.]{.takeaway .fragment}

## Time series carry an echo — the correlogram shows it

![Correlogram of U.S. real GDP-per-capita growth (T = 241). Bars outside the shaded band are statistically significant; a positive lag-1 value means fast-growth years cluster.](figures/fig_correlogram.png)

[Positive autocorrelation means consecutive observations aren't independent — so there is *less* information than the sample count suggests.]{.takeaway .fragment}

## HAC (Newey–West) SEs account for that echo

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-2|4-5|7|9|11-12|14"}
import numpy as np                           # numerics
from statsmodels.regression.linear_model import OLS as smOLS  # for HAC covariance

url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/data-open/master/AED/AED_REALGDPPC.DTA"
growth = pd.read_stata(url)["growth"].dropna()   # real GDP-per-capita growth series

n = len(growth); m = int(0.75 * n**(1/3))    # Newey–West lag rule m ≈ 0.75·T^(1/3) → 4

se_default = growth.std() / np.sqrt(n)        # assumes independence (too small here)

fit = smOLS(growth, np.ones(n)).fit(         # intercept-only model = the mean growth rate
          cov_type="HAC", cov_kwds={"maxlags": m})  # HAC-corrected covariance

print(se_default, fit.bse.iloc[0])           # HAC SE is LARGER — honest about serial dependence
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
The mean growth rate is fit as an intercept-only OLS so HAC applies cleanly. The HAC SE exceeds the
default precisely because positive lag-1 autocorrelation means fewer effective independent observations.
:::

## Prediction splits in two: the average vs. the individual

The same fitted line answers two different questions, with very different precision:

$$\underbrace{E[Y\mid X^*]}_{\text{average outcome}} \qquad\text{vs.}\qquad \underbrace{Y\mid X^* = E[Y\mid X^*] + u^*}_{\text{one individual outcome}}$$

[The individual carries an extra, irreducible term $u^*$ — the "$1+$" under the square root that **never** shrinks, even with infinite data.]{.takeaway .fragment}

## Predict a price — and both kinds of interval

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1|3|5-6|8-9|11-13|15"}
from scipy import stats                      # t-distribution for interval widths

fit = pf.feols("price ~ size", data=data)    # simple regression on size

x = data["size"].values; xbar = x.mean()     # ingredients for the SE formulas
Sxx = ((x - xbar)**2).sum(); n = len(data)

s_e = np.sqrt((fit._u_hat**2).sum() / (n - 2))   # RMSE — the irreducible noise floor s_e
pred = fit.predict(newdata=pd.DataFrame({"size": [2000]}))[0]  # point prediction at 2000 sq ft

t = stats.t.ppf(0.975, n - 2)                # 95% critical value, df = n − 2
se_cm = s_e * np.sqrt(1/n + (2000 - xbar)**2 / Sxx)        # conditional-MEAN SE
se_pi = s_e * np.sqrt(1 + 1/n + (2000 - xbar)**2 / Sxx)    # INDIVIDUAL SE (note the leading 1)

print(pred, t*se_cm, t*se_pi)                # point, CI half-width, PI half-width
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
Same point prediction (~$263k) for both. The only difference between se_cm and se_pi is the leading "1",
which is Var(u*). That one term is why the two intervals differ by ~5×.
:::

## The prediction interval is ~5× wider — and stays that way

![Panel A: the narrow 95% CI for the *average* 2{,}000-sq-ft price. Panel B: the much wider 95% PI for *one* house. The funnel widens away from the data's center.](figures/fig_ci_vs_pi.png)

[For a 2{,}000-sq-ft house: point ≈ \$263k · CI ≈ [\$253k, \$272k] · PI ≈ [\$213k, \$312k]. More data narrows the CI, barely touches the PI.]{.takeaway .fragment}

## A biased sample can break the line itself

::: {.incremental}
- **Selection on $X$** (e.g. oversample large houses) — OLS stays **unbiased** if $X$ is in the model; you only lose precision.
- **Selection on $Y$** (e.g. survey drops top earners) — OLS is **biased** for the population; needs sample weights, a Heckman correction, or a selection model.
:::

[No robust SE repairs a bad sample. Always ask whether the sample represents the population you care about.]{.takeaway .fragment}

# Best estimators, and the limits of a test {.divider background-color="#C21E72"}

[Act III · The resolution]{.act}

## OLS is "best" — until its assumptions fail

Under the classical assumptions, OLS is **BLUE** (Best Linear Unbiased Estimator) by the
Gauss–Markov theorem. When homoskedasticity or independence fails, OLS stays unbiased but
is no longer most efficient — **feasible GLS (FGLS)** can be tighter.

. . .

In practice, most applied work keeps **OLS with robust SEs**: the efficiency loss is small,
and a misspecified GLS weighting model can do more harm than good.

[Default to OLS + robust SEs. Reach for FGLS only when you trust the error-variance model.]{.takeaway .fragment}

## The bootstrap: let the data draw its own distribution

Instead of trusting a normal approximation, **resample the data with replacement** ~1,000
times, re-estimate each time, and read the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the resulting
coefficients as a 95% CI.

[The bootstrap assumes no normality and works for awkward statistics — ideal for small samples like these $n = 29$ houses.]{.takeaway .fragment}

## Every test trades off two ways to be wrong

| Decision | $H_0$ true | $H_0$ false |
|---|---|---|
| Reject $H_0$ | **Type I error** ($\alpha$) | Correct — **power** |
| Don't reject | Correct | **Type II error** ($\beta$) |

Tightening $\alpha$ cuts false positives but raises $\beta$ — fewer real effects detected.
**Power $= 1-\beta$** is the probability of catching a true effect.

[With only $n=29$, the bedrooms test failed to reject ($p=0.773$) — likely a Type II miss, not proof of "no effect".]{.takeaway .fragment}

## Power rises with effect size — and with the sample

![Power curve at $n=30$, SE $=15$, $\alpha=0.05$. Power equals $\alpha$ at $\beta=0$ and climbs toward 1 as the true effect grows.](figures/fig_power.png)

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1|3-5|7-10|12"}
from scipy import stats; import numpy as np  # distributions + numerics

alpha, se, n = 0.05, 15, 30                  # significance, hypothetical SE, sample size
tcrit = stats.t.ppf(1 - alpha/2, df=n - 1)   # two-sided critical value
betas = np.linspace(-60, 60, 500)            # grid of true effect sizes to evaluate

ncp = betas / se                             # non-centrality: effect in SE units
power = 1 - (stats.t.cdf(tcrit - ncp, n - 1) # P(reject | true β) under the alternative
             - stats.t.cdf(-tcrit - ncp, n - 1))

# here power reaches the 0.80 target only around |β| ≈ 44 — small effects need a bigger n
print(betas[np.argmax(power >= 0.80)])
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

## What to carry forward

::: {.incremental}
- OLS coefficients survive heteroskedasticity, clustering, and autocorrelation — the **SEs** need repair: HC1 / cluster / HAC.
- The fix is cheap: one `vcov=` keyword, or an intercept-only HAC fit for a time-series mean.
- Predicting an **average** is precise; predicting an **individual** is not — the "$1+$" floor is $\approx s_e$ forever.
- Selection on $Y$ **biases**; selection on $X$ only costs precision — robust SEs can't rescue a bad sample.
- OLS + robust SEs is the safe default; the **bootstrap** sidesteps normality; **power** decides what a null result means.
:::

# Trust the line, repair the uncertainty — and respect what a sample can't tell you. {.divider background-color="#C21E72"}
